questions.question: Monte Carlo waits for the episode to end. What is the smallest change that lets you update from a single transition (s, a, r, s')?
options: Buffer the transition and still update once the episode finishes
Use a model of the dynamics to compute the exact expected return in closed form
Replace the unobserved tail with γ times your estimate of s'
Average r over all transitions leaving s and use that as the value
questions.explanation: Substituting your own estimate for the part you have not observed yet is bootstrapping. It buys online updates and a big variance reduction, at the cost of bias while the estimate is wrong.

questions.question: What is the only difference between the Q-learning and SARSA updates?
options: SARSA needs a transition model and Q-learning does not
Q-learning maxes over next actions; SARSA uses the one actually taken
Q-learning requires a decaying α for convergence while SARSA works with a constant one
Q-learning updates at episode end while SARSA updates every step
questions.explanation: That one symbol decouples the target from the behavior policy. It is the whole reason one is off-policy and learns Q*, and the other is on-policy.

questions.question: With ε pinned at 0.1 forever, what does SARSA converge to?
options: Q* — ε only changes how quickly it gets there
Nothing; without decaying ε, SARSA has no fixed point at all
Q^π for the ε-greedy policy, short of Q*
The value of the uniform random policy
questions.explanation: On-policy means the exploration noise is inside the target, so the fixed point is the value of the policy actually being run. Only as ε → 0 does that fixed point become Q*.

questions.question: The max in Q-learning's target does something specific to noisy estimates. What, and what fixes it?
options: Underestimation; fixed by optimistic initialization
Overestimation; fixed by Double Q-learning's two tables
Divergence; fixed by adding a replay buffer
Excess variance; fixed by switching to n-step returns or TD(λ)
questions.explanation: E[max] ≥ max E, so taking the max over noisy values is biased upward. Splitting action selection from action evaluation across two tables removes the shared noise that drives the bias.

questions.question: On cliff-walking, Q-learning hugs the cliff edge while SARSA walks a row further away. Why?
options: SARSA's target prices in the chance exploration shoves it off
SARSA uses a smaller γ, so the -100 is discounted less
Q-learning simply has not converged yet on that task
SARSA initializes Q pessimistically in the cells adjacent to the cliff edge
questions.explanation: SARSA evaluates the policy it is really running, ε-noise included, so the expected cost of an exploratory step into the cliff is priced into the values. Q-learning's max prices the greedy path instead.

questions.question: Where do TD(0) and Monte Carlo sit on the n-step spectrum?
options: TD(0) is n = ∞ and MC is n = 1
Both are n = 1 and differ only in on-policy versus off-policy
TD(0) is n = 1 and MC is n = ∞
Neither is an n-step method; TD(λ) is a separate family entirely
questions.explanation: n is how many real rewards you collect before substituting an estimate: one for TD(0), all of them for MC. Deep RL usually lands between 3 and 20, and TD(λ) averages over all n with geometric weights.
